denominator: 176 retained parent teaching obligations, 19 bibliographic rows and 2 personal-case pointers excluded; 11 reviewer subclauses refine parents without adding points. Grouped requirements are not distinct concepts.
method: Coordinator read all 20 later lessons and complete original teaching differences, then compared actual canonical fields. Candidate exposure occurred before some field comparison; this is an agent semantic assessment, not a blind review.

requirements.heading: In one sentence
requirements.requirement: A chemical probe tests a mechanism; target engagement asks whether a compound reaches and interacts with its intended target under the measured conditions.

evidence.passage: A chemical probe is a research compound used to perturb a defined biological process in cells or animals. It is useful only to the extent that it is potent enough, selective enough and characterised well enough for the question being asked. Arrowsmith and colleagues put the requirement as a probe that is potent, of known selectivity and with a proven mechanism of action, and describe how many probes in common use were first characterised inadequately and later proved to be nonselective. LY294002 was described in 1994 as a selective inhibitor of PI3 kinase and was still sold as one by nearly all vendors, although by 2005 it was clear that it inhibited many other proteins at the concentrations used to inhibit PI3 kinase. An effect seen in cells at a high concentration therefore identifies an effect at that concentration, not necessarily a target.
evidence.explanation: Characterisation and the relevant experimental system determine whether a compound is a useful probe.

evidence.passage: Record the chemical identity, structure, source and purity, concentration-dependent activity, selectivity and effects in the relevant system. An inactive close analogue is useful, but its uptake or other properties may differ; an unrelated active probe can still share an off-target. Removing a whole protein can differ from inhibiting one function. Agreement among controls strengthens an inference in that system, and disagreement belongs in the evidence record rather than being discarded.
evidence.explanation: Characterisation and the relevant experimental system determine whether a compound is a useful probe.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Target engagement is not purified-protein binding, not function change, not downstream effect, not clinical benefit.

evidence.passage: Target engagement is the separate question of whether a compound interacts with its target where the experiment needs it. The cellular thermal shift assay, introduced by Martinez Molina and colleagues, is built on ligand-induced thermal stabilisation of target proteins and was used to monitor drug binding in cells and tissue samples; a shift can support engagement under the assay conditions and is not by itself an inhibition or occupancy percentage. Engagement, a change in target function and cell survival are three measurements, and an effect on viability does not identify the responsible target.
evidence.explanation: Binding, cellular interaction, function and outcome are distinct measured layers; a thermal shift is not inhibition or occupancy.

evidence.passage: Target engagement and the evidence ladder. Target engagement asks whether a compound interacts with its intended target in the relevant system. Binding to a purified protein does not show that the compound enters the cell or reaches its target in a tumour, and engagement is also not a change in the target's function, a downstream effect or clinical benefit. Each question needs its own measurement: engagement first, then a measured biological effect, then a check of the causal explanation with controls, then clinical evidence.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: A medicine needs product quality, PK, tolerability and evidence for the intended use; a good probe may lack delivery/stability/safety; an approved medicine can be a poor single-target tool.

evidence.passage: A probe is not a medicine. Arrowsmith and colleagues note that a probe does not need to meet the requirements of a successful medicine, such as good pharmacodynamics and oral bioavailability, and that high-quality probes have served as seeds for new medicines. A medicine also needs evidence in people about product quality, exposure, tolerability and benefit for its intended use, so a useful probe may lack adequate delivery, stability or safety, and an approved medicine can be a poor tool for isolating one target if several of its interactions contribute to its effects; this is an evidence-reading distinction rather than a claim that the same experiment establishes clinical suitability. A culture concentration is not a patient dose.
evidence.explanation: Product quality, exposure, tolerability and clinical evidence distinguish medicine suitability from research usefulness.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Mermaid: compound+controls -> engagement -> biological effect -> causal explanation; each question needs own measurement.

evidence.passage: Worked example, fictional. A new compound lowers the viability of cultured cells at 10 micromoles per litre, and neither engagement nor selectivity has been measured. The supported statement is that the compound has an effect in this culture at this concentration. It does not show that a particular protein is essential, and it does not show that a safe human dose reaches that protein. To close those gaps one would measure engagement and relevant selectivity, test an inactive analogue and a chemically different probe, and perturb the target genetically or by engineered resistance. Those steps address causality; exposure, quality, safety and clinical evidence remain separate questions.
evidence.explanation: The causal argument needs engagement, selectivity and independent perturbations before clinical evidence is considered.

evidence.passage: What to do next with a viability result. If a compound lowers viability in culture at one concentration, measure engagement and relevant selectivity, compare an inactive analogue and an independent probe, and use a suitable genetic perturbation or rescue; exposure, product quality, safety and clinical evidence remain separate questions that controls do not settle.

requirements.heading: Controls table
requirements.requirement: Three controls with limits: inactive close analogue (uptake may differ), structurally different probe (shared off-targets), genetic perturbation/engineered resistance-rescue (whole-protein removal != function inhibition). Record conflicting results.

evidence.passage: Controls carry the causal argument. An inactive or weakly active analogue from the same chemical family asks whether the effect follows the target-binding feature rather than shared chemistry; an active probe of a different chemical structure asks whether an independent perturbation agrees, with the limit that two probes can still share an off-target; and a genetic change or engineered resistance asks whether altering the target alters the effect as predicted, with the limit that removing a whole protein is different from blocking one of its functions. Workman and Collins add that a chemical probe can inhibit a specific function rather than remove the protein, which RNA interference cannot, and that both approaches have off-target as well as on-target effects. Agreement among these tests strengthens an inference, and conflicts should be recorded rather than set aside.
evidence.explanation: The three controls retain their uptake, shared-off-target and whole-protein-versus-function limitations.

evidence.passage: Controls and their limits. In chemical-probe practice an inactive close analogue serves as a negative control and a second, structurally unrelated probe reduces the chance of shared off-targets (Arrowsmith et al. 2015). Genetic perturbation is a separate line of evidence, with its own limit: removing a whole protein can differ from inhibiting one of its functions (the teaching lesson's reasoning, not a result read). The nearest real example is natural reversion: ovarian cancer lines from one BRCA2 mutation carrier acquired a secondary BRCA2 mutation that restored BRCA2 and went with resistance to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, and transient siRNA depletion of BRCA2 re-sensitised the restored clones (Sakai et al. 2009); that is natural reversion plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, and depletion is not pharmacological inhibition. Agreement among controls supports a mechanism in the tested system only.

requirements.heading: How it is measured
requirements.requirement: Observation card: input and consumption (heated aliquots consumed), conditions, output/units (soluble signal vs temperature or concentration at fixed temperature; deg C vs concentration axes differ), failures (detectability, baseline thermal behaviour, indirect complex effects; no universal shift cutoff).

evidence.passage: Reading a thermal-shift result. The cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples through ligand-induced thermal stabilisation (Martinez Molina et al. 2013). The readout is the soluble target signal remaining after heating, plotted either against temperature at a fixed compound concentration or against concentration at a fixed temperature, so degrees Celsius and concentration units sit on different axes and the two designs ask different bounded questions. A shift of the compound curve against a matched control supports engagement under those conditions; indirect stability or protein-complex effects can also change the signal, so it is not an inhibition or occupancy percentage, and no universal shift cut-off is given here. The heated aliquots are consumed, so a record should carry the compound, concentration, exposure time, temperature series, cell or tissue system and controls. In an isothermal-shift study with a pan-kinase inhibitor, a large share of non-kinase proteins shifted in cells, which the authors read as in-cell profiling being more likely than lysate profiling to identify indirect binding targets; they recommend lysate profiling to identify targets and in-cell profiling to verify intracellular engagement (Ball et al. 2020).
evidence.explanation: The two assay axes, consumed aliquots, signal units, detectability, complex effects and absent universal cutoff are stated explicitly.

evidence.passage: Record the named target and its detectability, baseline thermal behaviour, compound exposure, sample system and controls. In a temperature series, temperature changes while concentration is held fixed; in a concentration series, the selected temperature stays fixed. The output is soluble target signal, with different x-axis units in those two designs. Heated aliquots are consumed. An indirect stability change or protein-complex effect can alter the result, and neither a universal shift threshold nor a direct occupancy percentage follows from the plot.

requirements.heading: In one sentence / intuition
requirements.requirement: Combination = more than one treatment for a defined benefit that must be tested against an appropriate alternative with added harms; broader-population coverage can occur without within-tumour interaction.

evidence.passage: Reading a combination result. A combination rationale should name the job of each component (for example a growth pathway, a survival route, a location or stage, or a resistant population), and each story makes predictions that need testing. A regimen that beats one component does not show which component supplied the benefit, nor superiority to every alternative. In ASCENT-04 (443 people with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumours express PD-L1, combined positive score 10 or higher), median progression-free survival was 11.2 months with sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab and 7.8 months with physician's-choice chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio 0.65, 95 per cent CI 0.51 to 0.84; label section 14); that compares the ADC with chemotherapy as pembrolizumab's partner and does not by itself show synergy. Independent drug action offers another explanation: if each person benefits from the drug to which their tumour is most sensitive, patient-to-patient variability alone can explain the superiority of many approved combinations without additivity or synergy (Palmer and Sorger), which is an alternative explanation, not a rule that effective combinations lack synergy. A combination can also add toxicity, change exposure or force lower doses, and simultaneous and sequential treatment are different strategies that a molecular diagram cannot choose between.
evidence.explanation: Component jobs, population-level better-component coverage, correlation and shared resistance are separated from within-cell interaction and added harms.

evidence.passage: The two fictional comparisons use different units of inference. In a ten-tumour better-component model, A covers tumours 1 to 4 and B covers 3 to 6: 4 + 4 - 2 = 6 in the union, with four in neither group. There is no extra within-tumour interaction or added toxicity in that counting model. Separately, one cultured-cell experiment at 72 hours gives 20%, 30% and 40% inhibition for A, B and the pair at one fixed dose pair. Inhibition here is a reduction in vehicle-normalised viable-cell count, not a direct death measurement. HSA expects 30% and Bliss 44%, so 40% exceeds the first and falls below the second. Loewe needs single-drug dose-response curves; three numbers and no uncertainty estimate cannot establish a general synergy claim. In this model, greater overlap among responders reduces the union. Independent drug action does not require the two response groups to be statistically independent; shared resistance and response correlation matter to a population prediction.
evidence.explanation: Component jobs, population-level better-component coverage, correlation and shared resistance are separated from within-cell interaction and added harms.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Synergy = combined effect exceeds a stated reference model; stronger-than-either-drug is not automatically synergy.

evidence.passage: What 'synergy' means and how it is measured. Synergy is the narrower claim that a combined effect exceeds a stated reference expectation, and the references differ. Highest single agent (Gaddum) expects the better single effect and is the easiest bar to clear. Bliss independence expects the probability of being unaffected by each drug to be independent, so for effects written as fractions the expectation is A plus B minus A times B. Loewe additivity treats the two drugs as dilutions of one another and needs the full dose-response curve of each, with straight-line isoboles as its classic form. In Chou's median-effect method a combination index below 1 indicates synergism, equal to 1 additivity and above 1 antagonism, within that method only. Meyer et al. found no consensus on how to quantify synergy, and Yadav et al. note that a drug combined with itself can easily exceed the highest single agent and that their zero-interaction potency score is zero when both independence and dose additivity hold. A 2020 review's point stands: a synergy claim needs its model, scale and uncertainty named. Greco's 1995 review was identified but only its title could be read. Laboratory interaction analysis needs single-drug dose-response data, combination conditions, controls and variation estimates; a clinical survival advantage does not by itself measure a cell-level interaction.
evidence.explanation: HSA, Bliss and Loewe use different reference expectations and data requirements; a clinical benefit comparison is not a synergy assay.

requirements.heading: Reference-model table
requirements.requirement: HSA (larger single effect; no mechanism assumption; easiest bar), Bliss (A+B-AxB for fractions; independence), Loewe (dose-equivalence/dilution; needs full dose-response curves; CI<1 synergy); same data can be synergistic under one and additive under another; no consensus on the model; claim needs model + scale + uncertainty.

evidence.passage: What 'synergy' means and how it is measured. Synergy is the narrower claim that a combined effect exceeds a stated reference expectation, and the references differ. Highest single agent (Gaddum) expects the better single effect and is the easiest bar to clear. Bliss independence expects the probability of being unaffected by each drug to be independent, so for effects written as fractions the expectation is A plus B minus A times B. Loewe additivity treats the two drugs as dilutions of one another and needs the full dose-response curve of each, with straight-line isoboles as its classic form. In Chou's median-effect method a combination index below 1 indicates synergism, equal to 1 additivity and above 1 antagonism, within that method only. Meyer et al. found no consensus on how to quantify synergy, and Yadav et al. note that a drug combined with itself can easily exceed the highest single agent and that their zero-interaction potency score is zero when both independence and dose additivity hold. A 2020 review's point stands: a synergy claim needs its model, scale and uncertainty named. Greco's 1995 review was identified but only its title could be read. Laboratory interaction analysis needs single-drug dose-response data, combination conditions, controls and variation estimates; a clinical survival advantage does not by itself measure a cell-level interaction.
evidence.explanation: HSA, Bliss and Loewe use different reference expectations and data requirements; a clinical benefit comparison is not a synergy assay.

requirements.heading: Independent drug action
requirements.requirement: Independent drug action: person gets better of component outcomes; between-person variation can give group benefit with no within-person interaction; Palmer & Sorger 2017 clinical datasets, tumour models, simulations; alternative explanation, not rule; correlation and shared resistance reduce advantage; does not mean response groups are statistically independent.

evidence.passage: Reading a combination result. A combination rationale should name the job of each component (for example a growth pathway, a survival route, a location or stage, or a resistant population), and each story makes predictions that need testing. A regimen that beats one component does not show which component supplied the benefit, nor superiority to every alternative. In ASCENT-04 (443 people with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumours express PD-L1, combined positive score 10 or higher), median progression-free survival was 11.2 months with sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab and 7.8 months with physician's-choice chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio 0.65, 95 per cent CI 0.51 to 0.84; label section 14); that compares the ADC with chemotherapy as pembrolizumab's partner and does not by itself show synergy. Independent drug action offers another explanation: if each person benefits from the drug to which their tumour is most sensitive, patient-to-patient variability alone can explain the superiority of many approved combinations without additivity or synergy (Palmer and Sorger), which is an alternative explanation, not a rule that effective combinations lack synergy. A combination can also add toxicity, change exposure or force lower doses, and simultaneous and sequential treatment are different strategies that a molecular diagram cannot choose between.
evidence.explanation: Component jobs, population-level better-component coverage, correlation and shared resistance are separated from within-cell interaction and added harms.

evidence.passage: The two fictional comparisons use different units of inference. In a ten-tumour better-component model, A covers tumours 1 to 4 and B covers 3 to 6: 4 + 4 - 2 = 6 in the union, with four in neither group. There is no extra within-tumour interaction or added toxicity in that counting model. Separately, one cultured-cell experiment at 72 hours gives 20%, 30% and 40% inhibition for A, B and the pair at one fixed dose pair. Inhibition here is a reduction in vehicle-normalised viable-cell count, not a direct death measurement. HSA expects 30% and Bliss 44%, so 40% exceeds the first and falls below the second. requirements.heading: In one sentence
requirements.requirement: Dose = amount administered; dose intensity = amount delivered per unit time for a named drug and method.

evidence.passage: Amount, schedule and delivery are different questions. Dose is the quantity of drug and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024). Dose-dense scheduling shortens the interval, a dose reduction changes the amount, a delay lowers delivered intensity even if the eventual cumulative amount is unchanged, and omission lowers cumulative dose; a delay lowers dose intensity in the same proportion as an equal reduction (Alberto 1995). Planned and delivered intensity can differ: in a biweekly cisplatin study, delays of three or more days on 17 of 66 courses (26 per cent) left the mean delivered intensity at 83 mg/m2 per week, 88 per cent of the planned intensity (Kim et al.).
evidence.explanation: Amount, formulation, body-size basis, cumulative total, interval, delivered intensity, relative intensity and exposure are separate quantities.

evidence.passage: Dose intensity is the amount of a named medicine delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week. Relative dose intensity divides that by the intensity of a specified reference regimen. A combination average requires its declared method, such as the mean of the component ratios in Alberto's 1995 overview. Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity. Illness and toxicity can drive both modification and outcomes, so an observational association is not a causal effect of changing the dose. Bonadonna and Valagussa's retrospective 1981 CMF analysis associated benefit with at least 85% of the planned dose in that regimen; this was a dose-level finding, not a universal relative-intensity threshold or proof for other treatments.
evidence.explanation: Amount, formulation, body-size basis, cumulative total, interval, delivered intensity, relative intensity and exposure are separate quantities.

evidence.passage: Dose, dosage, cumulative dose and dose intensity are different quantities. Dose is the quantity of drug (state the drug, the formulation and whether it is per administration or per day; milligrams, milligrams per kilogram and milligrams per square metre are different scales), and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024, which says it does not specifically address several modalities). Cumulative dose adds the amounts given over a course. Dose intensity is the amount of a named drug delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week, and relative dose intensity divides delivered by a stated reference intensity, so it needs the reference regimen and method named; a delay lowers delivered intensity in the same proportion as an equal dose reduction, and the link between delivered intensity and response or survival has not been fully demonstrated (Alberto 1995). Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity, and a body-size-normalised dose is not a laboratory concentration. Teaching arithmetic with invented units, not data: four 10-unit administrations over a 4-week window give 40 units and 10 units per week; the same four over 8 weeks give 5 units per week, 50 per cent of the first intensity, which says nothing about benefit, exposure or safety.

requirements.requirement: Fictional Drug Z: four 10-unit doses; windows 0-4 wk and 0-8 wk with a declared final nominal interval; cumulative 40 both; intensity 40/4=10 and 40/8=5 units/week; with A as reference B is 50% intensity, not 50% benefit.

evidence.passage: In the fictional four-dose example, both schedules use the same Drug Z and formulation. The first window is week 0 up to week 4, with administrations at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3; the second is week 0 up to week 8, with administrations at weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6. Each declared window includes one nominal final interval and no administration at its right endpoint. Both totals are 40 arbitrary units, but the intensities are 10 and 5 units per week. A different final-cycle convention needs its own definition. Cumulative dose retains amount units; intensity adds a time denominator; relative intensity is the dimensionless ratio to a stated reference.
evidence.explanation: The declared final-interval convention makes equal 40-unit totals yield 10 versus 5 units per week, without halving benefit.

requirements.heading: Why it matters
requirements.requirement: Higher intensity not automatically better; observational comparisons confounded by illness/toxicity driving reductions; lower delivered intensity does not by itself explain an outcome.

evidence.passage: Planned versus delivered. Dose is the quantity of drug and dosage is the dose with its schedule (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024). A delay in the sequence of cycles lowers delivered intensity in the same proportion as an equal dose reduction (Alberto 1995), and planned and delivered intensity can differ: in a biweekly cisplatin study, delays of three or more days on 17 of 66 courses (26 per cent) left mean delivered intensity at 83 mg/m2 per week, 88 per cent of the planned intensity (Kim et al. 1993). An older, narrower finding sits beside the 2018 observational result above: in a retrospective analysis of adjuvant cyclophosphamide, methotrexate and fluorouracil for breast cancer, benefit was seen only at 85 per cent or more of the planned dose (Bonadonna and Valagussa 1981, abstract level, one regimen and disease), whereas Alberto found the link between delivered intensity and response or survival not fully demonstrated, with a threshold evident and no clear linear relation above it. That reductions are often made because of illness or toxicity, which can themselves affect outcome, is standard observational reasoning and is not attributed to these sources.
evidence.explanation: Observational intensity-outcome associations retain the reasons for dose changes and do not establish a universal causal threshold.

evidence.passage: Zhang et al. (2018) studied women diagnosed in Louisiana in 2011 with stage I to III breast cancer: 494 had hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease and 180 had triple-negative disease. Across five predefined cutoffs, their abstract reports that relative dose intensity below 85% was associated with worse overall survival in the hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative group (hazard ratio 1.93, 95% confidence interval 1.09 to 3.40). Cutoff findings differed by subtype: in the triple-negative group (180 women) 75% was the cutoff at which a higher relative dose intensity was associated with better overall survival (hazard ratio 2.39, 95% confidence interval 1.04 to 5.51), and the authors recommend keeping relative dose intensity at 85% or above in the hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative group and 75% or above in the triple-negative group, which is one registry's recommendation and not a standard. This adjusted observational association does not establish a universal dosing threshold or isolate the causal effect of a reduction from the reasons for it.

requirements.heading: How it is measured
requirements.requirement: Four-row quantity table: dose per administration, cumulative, intensity, RDI with example units and required context (window start/end, final cycle convention).

evidence.passage: Amount, schedule and delivery are different questions. Dose is the quantity of drug and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024). Dose-dense scheduling shortens the interval, a dose reduction changes the amount, a delay lowers delivered intensity even if the eventual cumulative amount is unchanged, and omission lowers cumulative dose; a delay lowers dose intensity in the same proportion as an equal reduction (Alberto 1995). Planned and delivered intensity can differ: in a biweekly cisplatin study, delays of three or more days on 17 of 66 courses (26 per cent) left the mean delivered intensity at 83 mg/m2 per week, 88 per cent of the planned intensity (Kim et al.).
evidence.explanation: Amount, formulation, body-size basis, cumulative total, interval, delivered intensity, relative intensity and exposure are separate quantities.

evidence.passage: Dose intensity is the amount of a named medicine delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week. Relative dose intensity divides that by the intensity of a specified reference regimen. A combination average requires its declared method, such as the mean of the component ratios in Alberto's 1995 overview. Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity. Illness and toxicity can drive both modification and outcomes, so an observational association is not a causal effect of changing the dose. Bonadonna and Valagussa's retrospective 1981 CMF analysis associated benefit with at least 85% of the planned dose in that regimen; this was a dose-level finding, not a universal relative-intensity threshold or proof for other treatments.
evidence.explanation: Amount, formulation, body-size basis, cumulative total, interval, delivered intensity, relative intensity and exposure are separate quantities.

evidence.passage: Dose, dosage, cumulative dose and dose intensity are different quantities. Dose is the quantity of drug (state the drug, the formulation and whether it is per administration or per day; milligrams, milligrams per kilogram and milligrams per square metre are different scales), and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024, which says it does not specifically address several modalities). Cumulative dose adds the amounts given over a course. Dose intensity is the amount of a named drug delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week, and relative dose intensity divides delivered by a stated reference intensity, so it needs the reference regimen and method named; a delay lowers delivered intensity in the same proportion as an equal dose reduction, and the link between delivered intensity and response or survival has not been fully demonstrated (Alberto 1995). Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity, and a body-size-normalised dose is not a laboratory concentration. Teaching arithmetic with invented units, not data: four 10-unit administrations over a 4-week window give 40 units and 10 units per week; the same four over 8 weeks give 5 units per week, 50 per cent of the first intensity, which says nothing about benefit, exposure or safety.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Three ABC pumps: P-gp/ABCB1 (taxanes, anthracyclines, vincas, MMAE in resistance models), BCRP/ABCG2 (topotecan, SN-38), MRP1/ABCC1 (anthracyclines, vincas, etoposide, methotrexate, conjugates).

evidence.passage: ATP-binding cassette transporters use ATP to move substrates across membranes. ABCB1, ABCG2 and ABCC1 can transport several anticancer drugs, with different substrate profiles. Their normal protective and excretory roles also affect absorption, distribution and drug interactions; transporter activity at the blood-brain or placental barrier is a different setting from activity in a cancer cell.
evidence.explanation: Drug-specific transport, normal barriers and mouse stem-cell protection are distinguished from acquired model resistance, clinical selection and inhibitor-development results.

evidence.passage: Acquired resistance can involve increased transport, but antigen loss, altered processing and other mechanisms must be assessed separately. Inhibiting a pump can change both tumour exposure and exposure in normal tissues. The unsuccessful clinical development of several P-glycoprotein inhibitors does not identify one universal reason for failure, and a resistant cell model does not itself select a treatment for a person.
evidence.explanation: Drug-specific transport, normal barriers and mouse stem-cell protection are distinguished from acquired model resistance, clinical selection and inhibitor-development results.

evidence.passage: Which pump handles which drug, and on what evidence. ABCG2 confers resistance to SN-38 and topotecan: in HEK-293 cells made to express wild-type or mutant ABCG2, cytotoxicity assays showed high resistance to mitoxantrone, SN-38 and topotecan and no appreciable resistance to etoposide or taxol (Robey et al. 2003), while in SN-38-resistant breast and gastric cell lines ABCG2 inhibitors restored SN-38 toxicity (Chang et al. 2016, SN-38 only). For P-gp, a brentuximab vedotin-resistant Hodgkin lymphoma line showed MMAE resistance and MDR1 upregulation, and 1 of 10 Hodgkin lymphoma patient samples expressed MDR1 (Chen et al.). Robey and colleagues' 2018 review describes ABCC1-mediated resistance to doxorubicin, etoposide and vincristine, transport of glutathione and glucuronide conjugates, and protective transporters at the brain and placental barriers. Zeng and colleagues' 2001 transport study also demonstrated MRP1 transport of methotrexate and folates, with polyglutamylation strongly limiting methotrexate transport. These are cell-line and overexpression models, not measurements of a tumour, and these laboratory findings do not validate a pump assay for selecting clinical therapy; Robey et al. 2018 describe efforts to make MDR1 a therapeutic target as unsuccessful so far. Normal-tissue protection also has experimental support: Zhou and colleagues found greater mitoxantrone sensitivity in Bcrp1-deficient mouse haematopoietic cells than in wild-type cells, supporting a protective role in that model. Robey's review also describes gastrointestinal transport affecting oral availability. These normal-tissue roles should not be confused with a cancer-specific mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Drug-specific transport, normal barriers and mouse stem-cell protection are distinguished from acquired model resistance, clinical selection and inhibitor-development results.

evidence.passage: Antibody-drug conjugates meet pumps after delivery. Direct transport by an efflux pump concerns a released payload that is its substrate, rather than export of the intact antibody-drug conjugate during endocytosis; A neighbouring cell could likewise export a payload that entered it, but a reduced bystander effect is a mechanistic hypothesis here, not a demonstrated clinical result. The absence of this efflux mechanism does not prove that delivery, release or target action succeeded; other barriers can remain. In breast cancer cells made resistant to trastuzumab deruxtecan or sacituzumab govitecan, resistance was mainly payload-specific, notably more efflux-transporter activity rather than loss of antigen, and ADCs with microtubule-inhibitor payloads restored activity in cells and animals (Rampa et al.); exatecan conjugates with a traceless self-immolative linker moiety overcame resistance of DXd and SN-38 conjugates in multidrug-resistance-positive models (Weng et al.). A study could compare intact ADC and free payload on the same cells, with and without a pump inhibitor, to ask which delivery step is affected. That comparison would still need controls for the inhibitor's other effects.
evidence.explanation: Drug-specific transport, normal barriers and mouse stem-cell protection are distinguished from acquired model resistance, clinical selection and inhibitor-development results.

requirements.heading: Common confusions

evidence.passage: How to read evidence about pumps. Pump RNA is not pump function: function depends on protein at the membrane and on whether a particular drug is a substrate. It is tested with fluorescent substrates that cells retain less when a pump is active, with and without an inhibitor, or by measuring intracellular drug; in SN-38-resistant breast and gastric cell lines, functional ABCG2 but not ABCB1 was found, and ABCG2 inhibitors restored SN-38 toxicity (Chang et al.). requirements.heading: Sources and scope
requirements.requirement: No pump measurement is a validated clinical selection test; five numbered sources.

evidence.passage: ATP-binding cassette transporters use ATP to move substrates across membranes. ABCB1, ABCG2 and ABCC1 can transport several anticancer drugs, with different substrate profiles. Their normal protective and excretory roles also affect absorption, distribution and drug interactions; transporter activity at the blood-brain or placental barrier is a different setting from activity in a cancer cell.

evidence.passage: Acquired resistance can involve increased transport, but antigen loss, altered processing and other mechanisms must be assessed separately. Inhibiting a pump can change both tumour exposure and exposure in normal tissues. The unsuccessful clinical development of several P-glycoprotein inhibitors does not identify one universal reason for failure, and a resistant cell model does not itself select a treatment for a person.

evidence.passage: Which pump handles which drug, and on what evidence. ABCG2 confers resistance to SN-38 and topotecan: in HEK-293 cells made to express wild-type or mutant ABCG2, cytotoxicity assays showed high resistance to mitoxantrone, SN-38 and topotecan and no appreciable resistance to etoposide or taxol (Robey et al. 2003), while in SN-38-resistant breast and gastric cell lines ABCG2 inhibitors restored SN-38 toxicity (Chang et al. 2016, SN-38 only). For P-gp, a brentuximab vedotin-resistant Hodgkin lymphoma line showed MMAE resistance and MDR1 upregulation, and 1 of 10 Hodgkin lymphoma patient samples expressed MDR1 (Chen et al.). Robey and colleagues' 2018 review describes ABCC1-mediated resistance to doxorubicin, etoposide and vincristine, transport of glutathione and glucuronide conjugates, and protective transporters at the brain and placental barriers. Zeng and colleagues' 2001 transport study also demonstrated MRP1 transport of methotrexate and folates, with polyglutamylation strongly limiting methotrexate transport. These are cell-line and overexpression models, not measurements of a tumour, and these laboratory findings do not validate a pump assay for selecting clinical therapy; Robey et al. 2018 describe efforts to make MDR1 a therapeutic target as unsuccessful so far. requirements.heading: In one sentence / intuition
requirements.requirement: Target = molecule/structure acted on; mechanism = how action produces effect; target name != reachable/driving/functional.

evidence.passage: A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.
evidence.explanation: Target identity, accessible exposure, mechanism, dependence, tissue selectivity and human benefit are separate claims.

evidence.passage: An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.
evidence.explanation: Target identity, accessible exposure, mechanism, dependence, tissue selectivity and human benefit are separate claims.

evidence.passage: The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

evidence.passage: Target engagement and the evidence ladder. Target engagement asks whether a compound interacts with its intended target in the relevant system. Binding to a purified protein does not show that the compound enters the cell or reaches its target in a tumour, and engagement is also not a change in the target's function, a downstream effect or clinical benefit. evidence.passage: Reading a thermal-shift result. The cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples through ligand-induced thermal stabilisation (Martinez Molina et al. 2013). The readout is the soluble target signal remaining after heating, plotted either against temperature at a fixed compound concentration or against concentration at a fixed temperature, so degrees Celsius and concentration units sit on different axes and the two designs ask different bounded questions. A shift of the compound curve against a matched control supports engagement under those conditions; indirect stability or protein-complex effects can also change the signal, so it is not an inhibition or occupancy percentage, and no universal shift cut-off is given here. The heated aliquots are consumed, so a record should carry the compound, concentration, exposure time, temperature series, cell or tissue system and controls. In an isothermal-shift study with a pan-kinase inhibitor, a large share of non-kinase proteins shifted in cells, which the authors read as in-cell profiling being more likely than lysate profiling to identify indirect binding targets; they recommend lysate profiling to identify targets and in-cell profiling to verify intracellular engagement (Ball et al. 2020).

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Controls (second compound, genetic perturbation, rescue) strengthen attribution but have limits.

evidence.passage: Controls and their limits. In chemical-probe practice an inactive close analogue serves as a negative control and a second, structurally unrelated probe reduces the chance of shared off-targets (Arrowsmith et al. 2015). Genetic perturbation is a separate line of evidence, with its own limit: removing a whole protein can differ from inhibiting one of its functions (the teaching lesson's reasoning, not a result read). The nearest real example is natural reversion: ovarian cancer lines from one BRCA2 mutation carrier acquired a secondary BRCA2 mutation that restored BRCA2 and went with resistance to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, and transient siRNA depletion of BRCA2 re-sensitised the restored clones (Sakai et al. 2009); that is natural reversion plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, and depletion is not pharmacological inhibition. Agreement among controls supports a mechanism in the tested system only.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: PK = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; dose vs exposure (named substance, named place concentration-time); route/organ function/interactions/product change exposure.

evidence.passage: Dose, exposure and effect are three different things. Dose is the administered amount; exposure is a named substance's concentration over time in a named place, which route, organ function, interactions and product properties can change for the same dose; and effect is a separate measurement, because effects or injury can persist after exposure falls and detectable drug does not guarantee productive engagement. Pharmacokinetics follows absorption (including how much of an oral dose reaches the circulation), distribution (plasma is not the unbound concentration inside a cell), metabolism (active metabolites may add their own exposure) and excretion, summarised by clearance, the removal relative to concentration, in volume per time. FDA labelling guidance lists the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) at the approved dosage, time to steady state, accumulation ratio, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life; this AUC is an exposure area and is unrelated to the area under a prediction curve that judges tests.
evidence.explanation: ADME and measured concentration-time exposure are distinguished from administered amount and pharmacodynamic effects.

evidence.passage: Read the measurement card as well as the curve. Record the dose, route, analyte, sampled compartment, assay, population and sampling interval. Concentration can be in ng/mL, maximum concentration in the same units, concentration-time area in ng·hour/mL, half-life in hours and clearance in litres per hour. Sampling should capture the phase of interest: a sparse late sample cannot reliably recover an unobserved early peak. Pharmacodynamics measures biological effects separately. First-pass metabolism can reduce oral bioavailability; protein binding and active metabolites also matter.

Dose is the administered amount; exposure is a named substance's concentration over time in a named place, which route, organ function, interactions and product properties can change for the same dose; and effect is a separate measurement, because effects or injury can persist after exposure falls and detectable drug does not guarantee productive engagement. Pharmacokinetics follows absorption (including how much of an oral dose reaches the circulation), distribution (plasma is not the unbound concentration inside a cell), metabolism (active metabolites may add their own exposure) and excretion, summarised by clearance, the removal relative to concentration, in volume per time. FDA labelling guidance lists the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) at the approved dosage, time to steady state, accumulation ratio, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life; this AUC is an exposure area and is unrelated to the area under a prediction curve that judges tests.
evidence.explanation: ADME and measured concentration-time exposure are distinguished from administered amount and pharmacodynamic effects.

requirements.heading: In one sentence / how it works
requirements.requirement: Two impairments together kill a cell though either is tolerated; one impairment may pre-exist and a drug can supply the second; two-loss does not need two drugs.

evidence.passage: Synthetic lethality is a lethal interaction between two impairments, each of which can be tolerated alone in the tested system. One impairment may already be present in a cancer and an experimental intervention can create the second, so the concept does not require two drugs. Genetic identity, loss of function, target engagement and the lethal outcome each need evidence.
evidence.explanation: Two tolerated impairments form a lethal interaction in a tested system; genetic labels, oncogene dependence, synergy and clinical response remain distinct.

evidence.passage: The 2005 Farmer and Bryant studies found sensitivity to PARP inhibition in BRCA-impaired experimental systems. Murai and colleagues later distinguished PARP trapping from catalytic inhibition. These findings support particular mechanisms; they do not make every BRCA-related finding a clinical selection rule. Candidate pairs such as MTAP with PRMT5, mismatch-repair deficiency with WRN, or repair deficiency with POLQ need their own model, exposure, selectivity and clinical evidence.
evidence.explanation: Two tolerated impairments form a lethal interaction in a tested system; genetic labels, oncogene dependence, synergy and clinical response remain distinct.

evidence.passage: What has to be shown. Compare matched cells with neither impairment, each alone and both, and check that the intended functions changed. Measure death separately from slower growth, because a viability signal can fall when cells divide less or change metabolism; pair a suitable death assay with long-term survival or colony formation, and record concentration, time and denominator, remembering that colony formation measures reproductive survival and not the way cells die. Synthetic lethality is not oncogene addiction, which is dependence on an active driver: in Src-, BCR-ABL- and EGF receptor-dependent cells, unequal attenuation of survival and pro-apoptotic signals after the driver is inactivated contributes to death (Sharma et al.). It is also not synergy, since a score above a reference model does not identify which losses interact. In the BRCA/PARP example, homologous recombination is a DNA repair process and HRD means deficiency of that process. Trapping PARP on DNA and inhibiting its catalytic activity are different perturbations, while repair restoration or changes in replication stress can change sensitivity. The first impairment can pre-exist, so a two-loss interaction does not require two drugs.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: Rescue: restore function and ask whether predicted harm falls; strengthens attribution when it works with controls; failed rescue not automatic disproof (expression, localisation, timing).

evidence.passage: Rescue, restoration and what each test can show. A rescue experiment restores a relevant function and asks whether the predicted harm falls; that strengthens attribution, but a failed rescue is not automatic disproof, because the restored function may not be expressed, localised or timed adequately (a reading rule, not a result from these experiments). A real example of functional restoration involved secondary BRCA2 mutations, often described as reversions. Ovarian cancer lines PEO1, PEO4 and PEO6 came from one BRCA2 mutation carrier: PEO1 was BRCA2 deficient and sensitive to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, while a secondary BRCA2 mutation that cancelled the inherited one arose in the patient (PEO4, PEO6) and, under cisplatin and PARP-inhibitor selection of PEO1, in the dish, restoring BRCA2 and resistance. Function was shown by homologous recombination assays after transfecting wild-type or mutant BRCA2 cDNA into reporter cells, and transient siRNA depletion (two siRNAs against a non-targeting control) re-sensitised the restored clones and PEO4 (Sakai et al. 2009). That is a secondary-mutation restoration plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, not a designed rescue of a knockout, and depleting a protein is not the same as inhibiting it with a drug. BRCA and PARP evidence is experimental: BRCA1 or BRCA2 dysfunction sensitised cells to PARP inhibition (Farmer et al.), BRCA2-deficient cells and tumours were acutely sensitive (Bryant et al.), and PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 and PARP2 on damaged DNA, with trapping potency (niraparib above olaparib, far above veliparib) not tracking catalytic inhibition (Murai et al.). Normal tissue can share the vulnerability: normal Brca2-deficient mouse intestinal epithelium showed very high apoptosis within hours of PARP inhibition (Hay et al.). None of this establishes clinical benefit.
evidence.explanation: Restoration can strengthen attribution; natural BRCA2 reversion and siRNA depletion are not designed rescue or drug inhibition, and failed rescue has alternative explanations.

requirements.heading: How it works
requirements.requirement: TI = ratio of dose producing a specified toxic effect to dose producing a specified useful effect; effect definitions/population/conditions travel with it; dimensionless; therapeutic window = range, different measurement.

evidence.passage: A formal therapeutic index divides a dose producing a specified toxic effect by a dose producing a specified useful effect in stated experimental conditions. It is dimensionless when the dose units are compatible. A therapeutic window instead describes a range of doses or concentrations meeting stated activity and harm criteria. Always retain the effect definitions, population, time and uncertainty.
evidence.explanation: An index is a dimensionless specified-effect dose ratio; a window is a range, and neither potency nor one assay proves general clinical safety.

evidence.passage: Low-concentration activity, target binding or a wider margin in a laboratory assay does not establish clinical safety. Distribution, formulation, schedule, other medicines and longer-term effects can change the relationship. The August 2024 FDA oncology dosage-optimisation guidance considers exposure, activity, safety and tolerability together, rather than assuming that the highest tolerated dose must be optimal. Its scope is stated for particular development settings and does not supply one rule for every treatment modality.
evidence.explanation: An index is a dimensionless specified-effect dose ratio; a window is a range, and neither potency nor one assay proves general clinical safety.

evidence.passage: A laboratory margin depends on which useful and harmful effects were tested, in which populations and over what time. A measure built on one toxicity can miss another. Different conditions in tumour-cell and normal-cell assays also limit transfer to people. A more selective result in one pair of cultures supports that assay comparison, not a general clinical safety claim. FDA's narrow-therapeutic-index discussion concerns small changes in dose or concentration causing treatment failure or serious harm; it does not classify all chemotherapy as one regulatory group.

requirements.heading: Why it matters
requirements.requirement: ADCs aim to widen the window but payload sets it; in one mouse study (Hamblett 2004) 2- or 4-loaded conjugates cleared more slowly than 8-loaded and had a wider index.

evidence.passage: Payload and loading change the margin. In one mouse study of anti-CD30 MMAE conjugates with 2, 4 or 8 drugs per antibody, the 4-loaded conjugate's antitumour activity matched the 8-loaded at equal antibody dose, the maximum tolerated dose of the 2-loaded was at least double that of the 4-loaded, which was twice that of the 8-loaded, and the 8-loaded cleared 3-fold faster than the 4-loaded; lower loading raised the therapeutic index for that conjugate (Hamblett et al.), which does not generalise to every ADC. FDA's August 2024 oncology dosage-optimisation guidance integrates exposure, activity, safety and tolerability, and says it does not specifically address radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapy products, oncolytic viruses, microbiota or cancer vaccines, or paediatric development.

requirements.heading: In one sentence / how it works
requirements.requirement: ADC toxicity follows the payload more than the antibody target; three routes: early linker release, target-independent uptake by healthy cells, target on healthy tissue (on-target off-tumour).

evidence.passage: Why ADC side effects follow the payload more than the target. Payload can reach healthy cells by early release from an unstable linker, by antigen-independent uptake (pinocytosis), or by the target sitting on healthy tissue; the Drago review concludes that off-target, off-tumour adverse events appear to dominate the toxicity profiles of most existing ADCs, while giving true on-target examples. A pooled analysis of ADC trials (Masters et al.; 43 studies with grade 3 to 4 data) found anaemia, neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy consistently reported with MMAE ADCs, thrombocytopenia and liver toxicity with DM1, and ocular toxicity with MMAF, and concluded the key toxicities are likely off-target and related to the payload. Those are patterns within published data with non-uniform reporting, and each product's own label governs its figures.
evidence.explanation: Payload-associated patterns and proposed exposure routes are separated from product-specific incidence, susceptibility and unsettled mechanisms.

evidence.passage: What the current labels report for the breast cancer products. Sacituzumab govitecan (SN-38 payload): neutropenia 64 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 48 per cent; febrile 6 per cent) and diarrhoea 62 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 10 per cent), with higher risk of neutropenia, febrile neutropenia and anaemia in people homozygous for UGT1A1*28. Trastuzumab deruxtecan: interstitial lung disease 12 per cent at 5.4 mg/kg, fatal 0.9 per cent. Datopotamab deruxtecan: interstitial lung disease 3.0 per cent (fatal 0.2 per cent) among 841 people with breast cancer, and 7 per cent in a pool of 484 with non-small-cell lung cancer. Trastuzumab emtansine: thrombocytopenia in 494 of 1,624 treated patients, grade 3 or higher in 145. These come from different trials and populations and cannot be compared head to head, a payload class does not make products equivalent, and a label rate is not a personal risk.

requirements.heading: How it is measured
requirements.requirement: CTCAE grade 1-5; ILD adjudicated by independent committee; free payload measured separately from intact ADC.

evidence.passage: The general CTCAE descriptions run from grade 1, mild, through grade 2, moderate, grade 3, severe or medically significant, grade 4, life-threatening, and grade 5, death related to the event. Not every grade is defined for every event. Seriousness is a separate reporting concept: a grade is not an attribution to the drug or a substitute for the event's specific criteria. Immune-effector syndromes can use ASTCT scales instead, so do not apply a generic five-grade ladder to every syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Event-specific grading, adjudicated lung disease and distinct payload/antibody measurements answer different safety questions.

evidence.passage: Label and trial figures differ by product, disease pool and definition. The trastuzumab deruxtecan label (5.4 mg/kg monotherapy pool) reports ILD in 12 per cent, fatal in 0.9 per cent, and DESTINY-Breast04 adjudicated 12.1 per cent with 0.8 per cent grade 5. The datopotamab deruxtecan label reports 3.0 per cent (0.2 per cent fatal) in 841 people with breast cancer and 7 per cent (1.7 per cent fatal) in 484 with non-small-cell lung cancer. The separate 15.4 per cent pooled-analysis figure below has another denominator and should not be compared directly. The datopotamab deruxtecan trials excluded people with a history of ILD or pneumonitis that needed steroids, so prior lung injury can bear on eligibility for later treatment.
evidence.explanation: Event-specific grading, adjudicated lung disease and distinct payload/antibody measurements answer different safety questions.

evidence.passage: For an antibody-drug conjugate, specify whether an assay follows conjugated antibody, total antibody, unconjugated payload or an active breakdown product. The 2024 FDA guidance defines total antibody as antibody with or without attached payload and discusses relevant constituent parts, metabolites and catabolites. Their concentration histories can differ: persistent antibody signal does not establish active payload in every cancer cell. Living cell products can expand or persist, and a radioligand combines radioactive decay with biological removal, so a freely circulating drug's half-life gives no universal clock for them.

requirements.heading: Figure + read-two-outcomes
requirements.requirement: Three panels: gut-brain nerve signalling plus blood-borne and learned inputs; reporting windows 0-24 h and beyond 24 h with overlap; nausea and vomiting as separate outcomes; no vomiting does not establish no nausea.

evidence.passage: Nausea and vomiting are different outcomes. Nausea is the sensation and vomiting the expulsion; they often occur together but one can occur without the other. Serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors and substance P acting at NK1 receptors contribute with other transmitters, and in two phase II cisplatin studies serotonin appeared to dominate early vomiting and substance P the later phase, with overlap (Hesketh et al.), so acute and delayed are reporting windows and not sealed pathways. The NCI PDQ classes are acute (the first 24 hours after chemotherapy), delayed, anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory and chronic; anticipatory nausea was reported in about 29 per cent of patients and anticipatory vomiting in 11 per cent, with prevalence varying with definitions and methods. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.
evidence.explanation: Separate gut/brain and learned pathways support overlapping timing categories; nausea and vomiting remain distinct outcomes.

evidence.passage: Gut-to-brain nerve signalling, blood-borne inputs and learned associations can contribute, so one blocked route does not account for every symptom. The timing terms organise observations. Acute commonly refers to the first 24 hours, delayed to symptoms beyond 24 hours, anticipatory to symptoms before treatment associated with previous experiences, and breakthrough to symptoms despite prevention. Learned symptoms are real; delayed does not mean mild, and early and later responses can overlap with multiday treatment. Prevention and treatment of symptoms that have appeared are different questions. In a fictional trial, no vomiting and no rescue medicine can meet its complete-response endpoint while the participant still reports nausea. Relief of either symptom does not measure tumour response.

The NCI PDQ classes are acute (the first 24 hours after chemotherapy), delayed, anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory and chronic; anticipatory nausea was reported in about 29 per cent of patients and anticipatory vomiting in 11 per cent, with prevalence varying with definitions and methods. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.
evidence.explanation: Separate gut/brain and learned pathways support overlapping timing categories; nausea and vomiting remain distinct outcomes.

evidence.passage: Gut-to-brain nerve signalling, blood-borne inputs and learned associations can contribute, so one blocked route does not account for every symptom. The timing terms organise observations. Acute commonly refers to the first 24 hours, delayed to symptoms beyond 24 hours, anticipatory to symptoms before treatment associated with previous experiences, and breakthrough to symptoms despite prevention. Learned symptoms are real; delayed does not mean mild, and early and later responses can overlap with multiday treatment. Prevention and treatment of symptoms that have appeared are different questions. In a fictional trial, no vomiting and no rescue medicine can meet its complete-response endpoint while the participant still reports nausea. Relief of either symptom does not measure tumour response.

requirements.heading: Why it matters
requirements.requirement: Navari 2016 randomised trial (untreated, highly emetogenic cisplatin or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin): no nausea assessed separately from complete response (no vomiting, no rescue); CR != no nausea; study-specific, not prescription. Other causes (medicines, constipation, metabolic) must be assessed.

evidence.passage: Reading antiemetic trials. In Navari et al. (380 evaluable chemotherapy-naive adults given cisplatin at 70 mg per square metre or more, or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin, all with dexamethasone, an NK1 antagonist and a 5-HT3 antagonist), nausea prevention was the primary endpoint and complete response (no emesis and no rescue medication) a secondary one. No nausea in the first 24 hours was 74 per cent with olanzapine against 45 per cent with placebo, while complete response was 86 per cent against 65 per cent, so a complete response does not mean no nausea, and a person with no vomiting can still have persistent nausea. MASCC and ESMO updated their regimen-specific guideline in 2023 (Herrstedt et al., published 2024). Read patient-reported nausea severity, vomiting episodes, rescue-medication use and the observation window together with the preventive regimen and adherence; symptoms that limit drinking or eating warrant prompt contact with the care team. This describes how to read endpoints, not a medicine schedule.
evidence.explanation: The named Navari regimen and endpoint definitions show why no vomiting/no rescue does not mean no nausea; patient reporting and alternative causes remain visible.

Signals from several cell types can contribute to fever, hypotension, hypoxia and other organ effects. Infection or other conditions can produce similar findings or coexist with the syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Multicellular inflammatory signalling is interpreted through clinical attribution, competing causes, treated denominator and product-specific observation, not a cytokine curve.

evidence.passage: Reading CRS without over-reading a cytokine level. CRS is a clinical syndrome, graded from attributed findings and not from a cytokine concentration. In a mouse model of CD19 CAR T-cell CRS, severity was mediated not by CAR T-cell-derived cytokines but by IL-6, IL-1 and nitric oxide from the recipient's macrophages, and IL-1 blockade abated it (Giavridis et al.); that supports a multicell amplification mechanism and does not show the same sources or shares in every human product. Infection and other conditions can cause or accompany the same findings, so the cause of a fever cannot be read from timing alone. A comparable report gives its grading version, observation window and treated denominator, with onset, maximum grade, interventions and resolution. Safety belongs to the product, disease, tumour burden and preparation, so experience with one blood-cancer product does not supply a solid-tumour product's rate, and no severe CRS in a small early study does not rule out uncommon events. CRS is a different problem from injury to healthy tissue that carries the target (on-target, off-tumour) and from neurotoxicity (ICANS). The treatment need not carry a cytokine payload to trigger endogenous inflammatory signalling. Tumour response does not establish acceptable inflammatory risk, and mild CRS does not establish lack of anticancer activity. Stopping a treatment input does not guarantee immediate removal of released signals or established injury. In a fictional early study, no severe CRS and a modest cytokine rise would not make every fever harmless CRS: attribution, clinical findings, a named grading framework, treated denominator and observation window are still needed.

requirements.heading: How it is assessed
requirements.requirement: ASTCT 2019 consensus, updated 2026: CRS definition requires fever at onset; grading centres on attributable hypotension and hypoxia including the support needed; fever need not persist after antipyretic or CRS-directed treatment for ongoing grading. Unresolved against primary text: exact fever threshold, whether 2026 changed the onset requirement or supportive-care terms.
remaining: Detailed ASTCT 2026 full text is access-blocked; 2019 criteria are explicitly attributed and supported.

evidence.passage: How CRS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. The definition requires a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher that cannot be attributed to another cause. Severity is then the more severe of two findings, again not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has neither. Grade 2 is low blood pressure that does not need vasopressors and/or oxygen by low-flow nasal cannula (up to 6 litres a minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 is one vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask or Venturi mask. Grade 4 is multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and/or positive pressure such as CPAP, BiPAP or intubation. Once someone has had a fever-lowering or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer needed to grade later severity: the grade then follows blood pressure and oxygen, and the person still counts as having CRS until the signs resolve. Organ toxicities linked to CRS are graded separately and do not change the CRS grade, and neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on the neurotoxicity scale, not added here. The 2026 ASTCT update (Perales et al.) convened experts to consider updating CRS, ICANS and haemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis-like grading, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it keeps, changes or relaxes any of these 2019 rules is not stated here; a report should say which version graded it.
evidence.explanation: The threshold, support categories and post-treatment fever exception are verified for 2019; detailed 2026 criteria remain inaccessible.

evidence.passage: The 2019 ASTCT consensus defines and grades CRS using attributed clinical findings, including fever at onset and the blood-pressure or oxygen support required. Its scale is a reporting framework, not a management algorithm. The 2026 ASTCT consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry; the numerical grading below is explicitly the 2019 version. Product, disease, preparation, observation window and treated denominator must accompany any incidence estimate.

evidence.passage: What is known about mechanism, timing and attribution. In 133 adults given CD19 CAR T cells, Gust et al. found that those with severe neurotoxicity had endothelial activation (disseminated intravascular coagulation, capillary leak) and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, and that the permeable barrier failed to protect the cerebrospinal fluid from high systemic cytokine concentrations including interferon-gamma. Higher risk went with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high marrow CD19-positive burden, high CAR T-cell dose, CRS and pre-existing neurological disease, and markers of endothelial activation before lymphodepletion were higher in people who later had grade 4 or worse neurotoxicity. That is an association in one product class and population, not a complete mechanism for every treatment. ICANS can accompany CRS or follow its own timetable, and neurotoxicity after CRS is scored separately, so recovery of blood pressure and oxygen does not show neurological recovery. If a person is confused while taking a sedating medicine and the ICE score falls, the grading rule requires that sedation be excluded, so the fall calls for clinical assessment, neither ignored nor diagnosed from the score alone. Clinical assessment also considers infection, metabolic disturbances, medicines and pre-existing neurologic disease. A safety report should retain onset, severity, attributed cause, interventions, duration, recovery and how many people were adequately observed. Separate fictional CRS and neurologic timelines can end at different times; they do not specify a typical order or duration. Stopping an engineered input does not guarantee immediate reversal of established neurologic injury.

requirements.heading: How it is assessed
requirements.requirement: ICE tasks: orientation, naming, commands, writing, attention; not whole neuro exam or stand-alone diagnosis; ASTCT 2026 separates monitoring tool from diagnosing ICANS; baseline matters; grading also considers consciousness, seizures, motor findings, brain swelling. Unresolved against primary text: ICE item scoring, grade thresholds, ASTCT 2019 vs 2026 grade criteria and the 2026 definition of other neurologic syndromes.
remaining: Detailed ASTCT 2026 full text is access-blocked; 2019 criteria are explicitly attributed and supported.

evidence.passage: How ICANS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. For adults, the grade is the most severe of five findings, none attributable to another cause. The 10-point ICE screen of orientation, naming, command-following, writing and attention scores 7 to 9 for grade 1, 3 to 6 for grade 2, 0 to 2 for grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable and cannot be tested for grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone who is awake with global aphasia can still be grade 3. Level of consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it: awakens spontaneously, awakens to voice, only to touch, or unarousable or requiring vigorous or repeated tactile stimulation. Any seizure that resolves rapidly, or EEG-only seizures that resolve with treatment, is grade 3, and prolonged (over 5 minutes) or repeated seizures without return to baseline are grade 4. Deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. Focal oedema on imaging is grade 3; diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad is grade 4; intracranial haemorrhage is excluded from ICANS grading. So ICE is a screen for encephalopathy and one input, not the whole examination: a person with an ICE of 3 who has a generalised seizure is grade 3, and headache alone is not a useful marker. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract adds categories such as non-ICANS neurological toxicities (parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsies, polyneuropathies) and tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity; their criteria, and any change to how ICE is used, were not readable here.
evidence.explanation: The adult 2019 ICE bands and other domains are explicit; a 2026 revision of detailed criteria or diagnostic use of ICE remains unverified.

requirements.heading: In one sentence / intuition
requirements.requirement: irAE = harm to healthy tissue attributed to treatment-related immune activity; the label names suspected mechanism, not organ, severity or treatment.

evidence.passage: Immune-related adverse events are injuries attributed to treatment-related immune activity, commonly discussed with checkpoint inhibitors. They can affect the bowel, lung, skin, liver, hormone-producing glands and other organs. A symptom or laboratory change during treatment does not by itself establish an immune cause.
evidence.explanation: Immune attribution is separated from occurrence, organ inflammation, severity, general checkpoint restraint and neighbouring effector-cell syndromes.

evidence.passage: What the label does and does not say. An adverse event is any unfavourable and unintended sign, symptom or abnormal laboratory finding that occurs during treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it; grading records that it occurred and how severe it was, and the clinical team assigns attribution to the drug, the intervention or something else (NCI Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program). An irAE is the narrower attribution of harm to treatment-related immune activity, so a symptom during immunotherapy is not automatically an irAE, and the abbreviation names a suspected mechanism, not an organ, a severity or a treatment. The SITC 2021 guideline uses the same wording, grades events including irAEs on a scale such as CTCAE version 5, and says that some irAEs need organ-specific management while overarching principles apply to all checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity. Checkpoint regulation helps limit responses against healthy tissue, part of peripheral tolerance; disrupting that protection can contribute to immune injury, but no single mechanism explains every event. Colitis names bowel inflammation and pneumonitis lung inflammation. A symptom or the suffix "-itis" does not establish its cause.
evidence.explanation: Immune attribution is separated from occurrence, organ inflammation, severity, general checkpoint restraint and neighbouring effector-cell syndromes.

evidence.passage: Timing and neighbouring syndromes. Immune-mediated reactions to PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies can occur in any organ system at any time after starting and can also appear after treatment stops (pembrolizumab prescribing information), so the infusion calendar does not define the observation window; onset differs by organ, with a SITC median of 5 to 10 weeks for diarrhoea or colitis and rash typically presenting 2 to 5 weeks after the first treatment. Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS after immune effector cell therapy are separate syndromes with their own ASTCT definitions and grading, not substitute labels for checkpoint-related organ injury, and stopping a treatment does not guarantee the immune effect has stopped.
